lines: Here, {gift_item}. Good things grow better when they are shared.
Take {gift_item}. Consider it a small harvest for the kindness you planted.
Good. {gift_item} took root with {tested_villager}. That is a healthy sign.
Then the advice sprouted. If {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}, that is a fair harvest.
Wrong soil for that seed. For {gift_subject}, plant {alternative_gift} instead.
{gift_item} did not grow there? Try {alternative_gift}. Some rows need different seed.

messages.text: Bad seed, bad soil, or bad advice. Hard to say. Plant {alternative_gift} next.
You harvested a frown from {gift_item}? Then sow {alternative_gift} and move on.

openings.text: Mind the fields. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to coaxing food from stubborn soil, then.

pacify.text: Fine. I will let the field lie quiet for now.
That is not enough seed for this row. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
No. You trampled too much for a handful of green to fix it.

lines: Dry rows and trampled crops teach a farmer to watch every footstep.
The soil's been kind lately. That's more than I can say for some visitors.
Seeds are small, but they know how to make a person wait.
Good rain is a blessing. Too much rain is work wearing a blessing mask.
A harvest is just a hundred small chores deciding to agree.
Bread starts long before the oven. Most good things do.
A good harvest keeps a village standing.
I once fixed a scarecrow so well it scared me at dusk.
One frost took half the field and taught the whole village humility.

lines.text: Stay off the rows if you can. The crops remember boots.
A carrot joke takes root slowly, if anyone lets it.
That thought came in muddy and left tracks.
I would not plant that opinion in poor soil.

lines: I remember waking like a field after frost. You gave the roots a chance.
You pulled me back from spoiled soil. I will not forget that harvest.
Your face is familiar, like a seed found in last year's coat.
I remember mud, hunger, and sunlight arriving too bright. Were you the sunlight?

lines.text: I remember you, but the memory still has grave dirt under its nails.

lines: Thunder shook the composter so hard the animals kicked at every thunderclap, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked fields, pens, and seed chests after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the composter, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the pens twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have pens to set right.
I checked hay bales and fence posts for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the hay bales after.
The rows can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the composter, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the composter, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the rows can wait; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the composter still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before fields, pens, and seed chests. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the fields and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the fields, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the composter first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the crop rows beyond the torchlight and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the composter enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a loaf of bread between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the composter, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand out of the wheat.
I checked fields, pens, and seed chests, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the composter, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a farmer which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the composter, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The rows can wait. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the fields found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the composter. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the paths to the pens and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the composter. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
